div1.head: Interview with John T. O'Donnell, Jr. [6/15/2002]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran John T. O'Donnell. Mr. O'Donnell served in the U.S. Army's 9th division, 47th infantry regiment. He served in North Africa, Sicily and Europe and his highest rank was T5. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. O'Donnell's home in Willoughby, Ohio during two sessions, one on May 29 and the second on June 15, 2002. John was 84 at the time of these recordings. Where were you living when the war started?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Pittsburgh, I was born in Pittsburgh, and I was inducted in Pittsburgh in June of '42.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: June of '42. Do you remember when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor, where you were?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No, it took me a day to sober up! (Laughter) We used to go out on Saturday nights and we got up -- I got up about noon time on Sunday and we heard about it. It didn't ring a bell too much until later on, but then everybody, there was a lot of people that they made a good war, and a lot of people volunteered and joined; be surprised at the number of volunteers that we had; quite a few of my good friends, young kids volunteered before they were out of high school. As soon as they got out of high school, they would take them in. They had no trouble.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you volunteer or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: I wouldn't volunteer for anything, because first, my mother and dad came from Ireland, Irish Catholics, and they hated the British, so my mother went -- she would have disowned me, I think, if I volunteered to begin with, but I didn't want to get killed, so I just let it go, and when I got drafted, I decided I'd make the best of what I had, whatever came along, and it worked out pretty good for me. It was a good experience, if you lived through it, without being torn up too much. And I found out that the Germans were, my mother was wrong about the Germans; that they were mean people, especially under Hitler.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were inducted in June of '42?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Then we were trained in what they call heavy weapons for infantry which is the 81 mm mortar. They weigh about 8 pounds. It's a powerful thing, and the old World War I water cooled machine guns, 30 caliber, and after we finished our basic training, we were put on the old railroad cars and ended up at Fort Bragg, and they were out in the fields in pup tents and we were with them for about three weeks, and then they put us on another train, and we went up to Newport News and went up the gangplank, and when we get out in the ocean for a while, we were told where we were going. There were all kinds of rumors. They even gave us physical inspections, when we're 20 days out, and the things for venereal disease, but these old timers that were with the 9th Division and took the two years amphibious training, they were moaning all the time. "Look where what they sent us -- guys that never saw an amphibious boat or anything like that," which was the truth, and we were supposed to have that little 03 gun that would take 30 shells, that you would carry with that, because we were assigned the job of being munition carriers for the air cooled machine gun, the same bandolier.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go overseas? When was this?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: My birth date, October 8, we got on the boat, and we went up and down the coast and then for November, November 6 or 7, they all met and gathered together. Our outfit went to the southern part of French Morocco, a town called Safi.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This would be in '42?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: '42, yeah. October or November 8 was the invasion day. Some went through the Straights of Gibraltar and landed in Algiers, Oran, that was about it. Then there were some outfits that landed in Casablanca, Port Lyautey, the capitol of French Morocco and we were the southern most invasion on Safi, French Morocco, and our job was to land the 2nd Armored Division, who would be replacement for the 1st Armored Division because they got pretty well beat up by the Germans, and from there, they said that the Arabs would unload the supply ships, and after about a week and a half, they didn't have half of the ship unloaded. They couldn't get them to work, so they asked for volunteers, so we all volunteered and went down with the Jeeps and when you'd run into a food hold, you would blow the whistle and load it up and take the food and supplies and that up to where the company was. But to get back to the invasion, they loaded us on these little wooden landing craft infantries. You put a platoon in there, and these 17, 18 year old kids in the Navy, they didn't give a damn about anything. They would ram them up on shore. We would have to push them back out, but the recon said that we had a cliff about 40 foot high to scale. Well, it turned out to be there were three cliffs about 400 foot high. Like it always reminds me of they are saying some day that California will fall into the ocean. That's what happened there. It took us about five hours to scale the -- get up to the top where the French guns were. And the beautiful thing about it was we had the New York battleship as support, and the second round that they fired, and I don't know how they could ever figure it out, but the second round they fired, the commander of their garrison, there was 500, 20 mm guns and a command post, and it was controlled by the commander of the garrison, and they shot one, landed on this stone. Everything was stone around there. And right up, took him out of the command seat. So all we got was 50 mm guns and so on, and no problem, but all the big artillery was gone. The only scary part was the first day, or night, the rumors were that their infantry, with these white Arabian horses, were going to come up and try to kick us back down into the ocean, but that never happened. Then the French capitulated. They had sent one of the Clarks, three or four days before the invasion, actually, and they start negotiating, and the only thing is the Germans weren't around that part, even. So we stayed around Safi for a few days because they put some -- two companies, L and M, I think it was, up from the 3rd Battalion of the 47th Infantry. They put them on ships, and they went right into the harbor, and took it over without any problem at all, and they were able to unload the armor, without any problem and when they got them all unloaded and they decided they wanted us up around Casablanca, and the capitol of French Morocco, and our battalion commander, a fellow by the name of Colonel Randall, he says, "I have orders to get you guys up to Port Lyautey," which is the capital of French Morocco and he said, "I have three different ways I could get you there. We can get on a train and ride. We can get on the trucks and drive up there," because it was approximately 250 miles, "or we can walk," so he says, "you know what it's going to be. But the reason we're going to walk, you'll need it to be in shape." And we walked, 22 to 23 miles a day, until we got to Casablanca. That was about the 20th of December, and we put on a parade and things like that, and right in the middle of town, we took a pee break. Every man went up against the buildings, but then we went to Port Lyautey, and the only thing that I remember so much about that is Churchill, Roosevelt, and I think it was Kruschev, I'm not sure, they had a meeting there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Stalin?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, Stalin it would be. And the three of them were there, and they had us out in the swamps to guard them. Outside of that, it was uneventful. We were bivouacked in an oak forest which they would strip off the bark of these oak trees and use them for the -- to make corks for the wine. They made nothing but good wine there, and we could buy a 5 gallon can of wine for a dollar, until they start running low on it, then they were selling you almost wood alcohol, because you got to age the wine, and that's when I quit drinking in North Africa! Or you would end up blind! Then they moved us up to Oran. We were the first troops to ride the 40 and 8 cars that they had in Europe. 8 horses or 40 men. Well, we carried barracks bags and so on. There were about 32 people to one of the trains, or cars. They are narrow gauge trains and everything else, and they would stop every once in a while to let you out, take a break to relieve yourself, and stretch your bones a little bit, and then from there, we hiked into Tunisia and our first good combat was a place called Port Lyautey and we were at the foothills and the Germans were up here about three thousand in the Atlas Mountains. You couldn't move during the day. They had every inch of ground covered. If you moved, in 2, 3 minutes there would be a shell come down and get you. Casualties were fairly heavy. You would dig a slit trench. We never drug what they called a fox hole which was a hole about this and that. You couldn't dig down that deep. It was all granite, I guess, barren, and a very good friend of mine was laying in one of these slit trenches, as we called them, and a shell come down and took his head off, and that would make you want to go and fight, to charge after them, but you think about it. It was pretty hard to take. We were in that position, in Port Lyautey for close to 26 days, and I don't know if your dad ever told you about the rations that you had in those days. You had baked beans. Dog food, something like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Spam?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No, that was good food compared to what we had. We had three different foods, and it got to the point, I was down to one can a day, and I had a class ring of my brother's that he gave me to wear, and the reason he did that, the girls at that time were out to get all the class rings they could get from the boys that were around, and he said, "I find it hard to say no." I lost it there somewhere. So somewhere in Port Lyautey is my brother's class ring. And then we moved on from there and got into Sedjenane, and it was in Kasserine Pass where I got wounded. I got a mortar fragment in through here, and I had to walk approximately four to five miles out of the mountains. Everything was mountains there, Atlas Mountains. It was barren, nothing. I walked down with another fellow, and we get in the first battalion medical tent and the doctor that looked at me, he had a little metal probe, and he went in there and he said, "What did you get hit with?" I said, "It was mortar, we were under mortar fire." He said, "Boy, this thing feels almost like it's a bullet, it's so uniform." He said, "If you let me," he said, "I'll freeze it and see if I can bring it back out the same hole," he said, "because under here, there's a lot of nerves and you don't know what the hell would happen." I said, "Go ahead. " So he froze it, and it took him about 15 minutes to get it out, and then after that, they loaded a bunch of us back up into a truck back to Oran to what they call a station hospital, and I spent about three weeks there. Then we found out that our outfit was bivouacked on the beach in Oran so we took off and went to our outfit and a good friend of mine that I used to loaf with a lot had joined the Navy, and here he come up and visited us one day. And in fact, I had, during the whole war, I had a friend of mine that was from the gang that we loafed with, he got into the field artillery, and he was shipped over to England for going across the channel by the name of Franie Martin. He came and visited us, visited me. My brother visited me the day or two days before I was scheduled to go home on that point system they had, because I had 138 points with, you get five points for each battle star, five points for each wound. They didn't give you anything for the good conduct medal, but I got five points for the other star -- what they call that -- this one here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bronze star?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, the bronze star, and then one and a half point for every month overseas and I had more overseas time than -- I had just a little shade over four months in basic training, and the rest was two years and something overseas. But from there, they sent us down, about 100 miles south of Oran, and the edge of the Sahara Desert, and they said, "You're going to be going into Sicily and we want to get you used to walking because that's all you can do in Sicily." Mountainous and everything else, so they decided they'll do the 100 miles in 48 hours, with no stopping or anything like that, and I don't know if you ever heard of Sciroccon winds. The wind was hotter than what the sunshine and that was, and it was, I never saw anything so hot in my life, but you don't weigh anything, you know. I went down to about 140 pounds, when I was 173 at the start of going into El Guettar, and we went to, we got on a ship, took about eight days before they secured everything at Palermo, the capital city of Sicily. We landed in there, and from there we went and started walking and ended up in a place called Randazzo, and we got squeezed out by our 60th regiment, some of the units of the 1st Division and the 45th Division, and we ended up down in Mount Aetna, and the only thing that I couldn't figure out, when we were there, it was like you were sitting on a pile of asphalt, and they said that Mount Aetna was an inactive volcano, 8000 feet high, and after we got out, about a year later, it became active again, and it stayed active for quite a few years, and the last I heard of, it's 11,000 feet high now. We were bivouacked after the Germans gave up, because it's the first place I saw that P51 in action, and we went up a mountain, curved around a mountain like that, and I must have counted a thousand German vehicles that were taken out by strafing by the P51. There was nothing that could touch them at the time. And when we were in north Africa, we went back at night time to get water and rations because the Germans with their Stukas dive bombers and so on, you couldn't move. You had to stay under cover or dig a good deep hole and pray that they don't drop anything in the hole. After that was over, they put us in a town called Cefalu. They talk about it in this book here. Our division commander, Major Craig, he was Catholic, and in Cefalu, there was a cathedral built in the 1400's, a Catholic cathedral right on the ocean and we used to go to mass there. The only thing about it that is different than our church, only the rich people had chairs, and they had their names on it, and so on. The only place, if you want to go to town and have some fun, you had to go to Palermo, so they would take you down in the morning and bring you back at night. It was around, close to 40 miles away. This lasted for a while, then they decided they had to break the troops out of the beachheads in Italy and they loaded us on what the British called, like our big largest in the river barges. These were only bigger and you could put about 600 men standing up on that thing, and we got on there, and got about halfway to Italy, and they said, "We're going to turn around and unload you." They broke out of the beachhead. Oh, that was great. But then the word come down that us and the 1st Division were going to England for, get ready for the invasion across the channel, so they took us two weeks to go, and we landed at Liverpool, and then they took us from, when we debarked at Liverpool, got on a train, and everything has to go to London and then back out again, and we went to Winchester was where the division was. But three of the companies in the 47th stayed at a place, Tichborne estates, Lord and Lady Tichborne lived there, but he was with the 8th Desert Rats in North Africa, and I don't know where she stayed, but it was, and I was in company headquarters then, and we stayed in the manor house, and then they come up with these Quonset huts and that's where the three companies stayed there. It's a matter of having enough money to enjoy yourself, as we had guys that couldn't hold themselves. They drink four beers and their beers were 14 percent, and you know what we have in this country! (Laughter) And they couldn't hold themselves, until they got used to it, and then the British bartenders would usually shut you off after two pints, and we learned to shoot darts. I was pretty good at darts. Then nobody was allowed to go on a furlough and this first sergeant of ours, Larry Croban, he told the company commander, he said, "We met a couple of girls that live in Wexford, Wales," and it didn't cost you anything to ride the trains. We went in the subways, you could just get on them and I guess they kept track some way, but the United States government paid for all that, and we paid five cents a carton for cigarettes in England, so I said to them, I said, "Well why don't we take a book of 72 hour passes. I can sign the company commander's signature," and we mentioned it to captain M, and he said, "Okay but you got to call in every day." We were on six hours notice for things. We went there and we stayed for about four 72-hour passes and then we ran out of money so we come back to the company and we made a couple dry runs down to the beach. In fact, they wanted to make the invasion around the third or fourth, somewhere around that, and we were on the liberty ships, because we were coming in about the fourth day, D plus 4 or 5, something like that, and then the channel waters kicked up and they called it off, and there was a big debate about whether they were going to do it on the 6th, but Ike decided, took a chance, and the weathermen said there is going to be a short period when he knows it will be okay. So we were on the liberty ships and comes D plus, will be run the 10th or 11th, something like that, but they dropped us off in water about this deep, walked ashore. Everything was cleared, and we went in the vicinity of Saint Marianglas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What beach did you land on?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Utah. The other ones, the Army screwed up on that. They were supposed to keep -- or the Air Force -- they were supposed to keep bombing and they didn't. They cut it off about an hour beforehand. That's why they got the hell knocked out of them. Some of the outfits, I met some kids from the 16th Infantry of the 1st Division and they got knocked out of the compound, it was so bad. We didn't lose anybody until about D plus 12 or 13, and then we were halfway across the peninsula, and our first casualties, first five, were we had 12 B47's as air support, and every morning, the company commander would go to a commander's meeting and they would get targets, and they had a couple people that carried these colored things about this square. You would lay them in the ground when you were there, so that your Air Force would see that, and they wouldn't bomb you, or strafe you, but nobody told them that anybody was going to be as far advanced as we were, and there was these two hedge rows, you probably heard enough about them, but like me and the rest of the company headquarters was on this one and then there was one over here and they were strafing here and there, but mostly here, and there were five guys that were wounded with the 50 caliber machine guns. Nobody got killed. In fact, we had a kid from McKeesport PA, called Luke Savage. He was a law student at Duquesne University. He was 6'5" and he could run like the pros do today. He got a wound on his calf, on his hip, just grazed, and one right here, three of them, enough to put him in the hospital for a while. And they wanted to give him a purple heart. And he says, "What? I wouldn't take a purple heart getting wounded by my own people." [ LAUGHTER ] Until we found out about the point system, then he went and got his purple heart, but there are a lot of funny things happened, you know. But it took him out of combat for a while, but he became a very good friend of mine, and towards the end of the war, we took over breweries. They had the officers' clubs which the enlisted people weren't, so then they would go and take over a brewery and have the bar and everything set up, and we had a little Jewish fella that was battalion sergeant major. I never saw a mind like he had. He knew everybody in the whole goddam regiment and I became pretty good friends of his because I could talk to him. I could even call him a Jew if I wanted to, and he wouldn't take offense to it, but he used to call me up. See when I got into company headquarters, I was able to type and where I used to work in Pittsburgh, if a boss was off, I could take his job and do the work, and you had to do a lot of clerical work, and he would call me and he'd say, "John, I need four guys for duty," and I'd say, "Good or bad? " If he'd say good, I would send friends. If he said bad, then I would send the fuck-ups, which it happened good that way, but he could remember everybody. I thought I was pretty good. I used to do those rosters, I'm showing you there. Fifty percent of those names on there I had memorized. I could sit down and type, when I would come to these guys. The secret of it was you listened or you recalled what state they came from. If they came from Ohio, you started with 34. You come from Pennsylvania, you started with 33. Like mine was 33-28-03-05. That is the only, that and my social security number, are the only two numbers I can remember now, but down in the East Coast was 32. And up in New England was like 11 and 12 and 13, and something like that, then the farther west you went, the higher the first two numbers went.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you become a clerk? You were an ammo carrier first?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: I was an ammo carrier, I was a machine gunner, I never got to be a mortar. The casualty rate with mortars, they're back a little farther, but yeah, so I didn't get into clerking. When Croban got it, he said, "I know how to do it," he says, "but I don't have time to do it." You had to turn in what they call a morning report, every day, and if you get replacements, which we got from the time I took over until the war was over, we had 1,500 different kids go in through our company. We had 196 that I know, I could show you in here, I X'd off the ones that I knew that were killed in action, just from B company, 47th Infantry. But this Croban and I were bosom buddies, up in the hills, up in Kasserine. We used to sit, nothing happening, and talk about making movies. There were a couple cartoons, that who was it used for, like for, let's see, one of the civil war -- hell -- it's like we decided that Clark Gable was the right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Gone With The Wind?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Gone With The Wind, that he was the right one and so on, and we became very good friends, and here, come on in here, I'll show you a picture.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's talk about the Normandy breakout. We didn't get that on tape.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Oh okay. That was fascinating. The bombing, I told you about that, and our 3rd Battalion was supposed to ride the tanks and they got crippled so badly that they brought in the 1st Battalion, our battalion.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me, I don't think we got that on tape. Tell me again how that happened?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Okay they were bombing perpendicular to the line, instead of going parallel, and it was a windy day, and the artillery shot the smoke shells, and the smoke was drifting back, and we got hit worse than the Germans got hit, basically, but our battalion was a little bit back and out of the way, but they went as far back as eight miles, and then, when the breakout come in, one thing I got to make sure that I remember to tell you is they used to say the cowards were never in combat. They were the truck drivers that took you, and we went as high as 100 miles some days. It would be amazing, you would ride with, on these tanks, and they'd get maybe 80, 90 miles in one day, and fields all around there are loaded with gasoline supplies and all that. They had what they called the red ball and the blue ball highway. The red ball, you went towards Germany. The blue ball, you come back to Cherbourg and get loaded up again and they were on their own, nobody to check them or that, because if you wanted to make that kind of mileage, you had to cut corners, and the drivers were all quarter master guys, and they were all colored, and they were just as exposed as we were, and the reason for putting troops on the tanks, if you did run into any resistance, the tanks would pull off. The infantry would get out and get ready and have a firefight, and usually disperse, and some of the men get back up on the tanks and keep going until they ran out of gasoline, or until the gasoline caught up with them. And they went across from, let's see, see here is Utah beach. We went on up, and we were the 1st Division in Cherbourg and this is where Ernie Pyle was with us. But where is St. Lo?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me again about Ernie Pyle. I don't think we recorded that on tape.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Well, he came along. I don't know where.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to him at all?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. He was talking to Lieutenant Shockley here, and I was, stayed with the lieutenant, and then anything that happens, I would record it, and then send, incorporate it in my morning report. And one thing about it, at one time, when they start breaking up, I had six first sergeants in our company, and they had to come to me to know what to do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your highest rank was T5 then?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Do I what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Your highest rank was T5?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Sure, I wouldn't take any higher, because if you took any higher, you were going to be up in the front.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They allowed you to refuse the promotion?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Sure. At one time, we had a lieutenant, and he became the assistant company commander, and this is shortly after we got into some heavy combat going up towards Cherbourg, and he would say, "Where is Lieutenant Hagan?" I said, "He's probably back at the aid station." He said, "What do you mean?" I said, "Every time we run into combat, he runs a fever and he goes back to the aid station and they send him out of combat for a couple days." As soon as the combat is over, he's fine again, and he said, "Well then I'm going to make you my" -- it's still a lieutenant, "second lieutenant." You'd know it, what it is, but if the company commander is not there, he takes over, and he said, "Then I'll make you my officer." I said, "No you won't." I said, "I'll do my job for you just the way I've been doing it." Croban taught me that. He wanted them to give him a field promotion a long time before, then towards the end of the war, they wanted to give him a field promotion, he said he wouldn't take it. He had that right, and they were only temporary anyway. When the guy that had the T5 got hurt, then they gave me that, but then when they were sending them home, they used to give them high ranks so they froze all that on anybody they were sending home, or everybody would be first sergeants when they got their pension. That was the idea of that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So do you recall any conversations you might have had with Ernie Pyle?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: I was kind of bashful with him. And he was talking, there's a bunch of guys that I could show you the roster that I have, and that he would talk to the guys. Where are you from? There was a sergeant, Red Hamilton, from Philadelphia. Then there were three or four kids that had had some rank from Pittsburgh. Pittsburgh, Butler, a few of those western Pennsylvania towns where it made up a big part of the 9th infantry division. But not too much. He asked me my name and so on, but he was always taking notes, and his act or writings, what the people were doing, were pretty accurate as far as I could tell.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. So after the Normandy breakout, what happened next?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Then we went to -- our outfit went to Brussels. Liege is the town that we went through, and then from there, we went through the Siegfried line here. See all the concrete that they used?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: But they couldn't put these things across the road. You had to move them. And the only thing is, they had pill boxes all over the place, and some people, they had the right kind of eyes, they could look and they could tell and they were camouflaged to look like they were homes or cottages, and this one kid from Texas, Busby was his name, would say, "That's a pill box," and the guys would go up there and they always had blind spots. You would get somebody to go figure out the blind spots. They would go up and they would drop concussion aid and reach down the air conditioning, and people would come out and give up to you, or else you'd bring up a 155 howitzer and bang that at the front door and it would get them to come out. Because we had, in the Battle of the Bulge, which was shortly after -- well this led to the Hurtgen Forest, when they went through there, and then Montgomery wanted some ammunition so he could beat the Germans, and we weren't allowed to fire on the Germans, in the Hurtgen Forest and we took a hell of a beating in there, an average of one or two guys a day, and the thing with the Forest that you had to dig a big platoon or squad bunker and they would dig it about 12 by 12 and go down maybe 6 foot, and then they would cut logs from these trees, put them across, throw dirt on top of that, put another set of logs, and it would take a direct hit. But if you were outside and they hit in a tree, you know what it's going to be like. You take a hose and squirt it up in the tree, and this sergeant Croban got hit that way, and he ended up going back to the states, married his girlhood sweetheart and then they sent him down to Atlantic City to rest and recuperate which was nice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah!

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: And him and I and Ann and his wife, we used to get together on Memorial Day and Labor Day, until we started having children. That took care of that, but we did it, three or four years, we got together like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything else about the Hurtgen forest campaign?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. The company stayed, the headquarters was in a little farmhouse, and they raised these pure white geese and you could not get near that farmhouse without the geese shhhhh (indicating noise) and they Would attack you if you would keep coming at them, but the thing about the Hurtgen Forest, I have a book on it by somebody from the 8th division. They got the hell beat out of them up there. I never heard of the 8th Division until my brother sent me this book on Hurtgen Forest, from California, but there was the Hurtgen Forest, where we were, and then you had a field that was a plain, probably 500 yards, and then a town called Gresnovich (ph), and this sergeant McConnell, he said to me, "Do you think I could talk to the company commander? I want to get transferred to the artillery." I said, "Why?" He said, "Well them son of bitches, I've been calling in targets for them and I could see the Germans building up, and they want me to go across that field. They're crazy." Company commander transferred me, and he had been all through, and a platoon sergeant for, ever since I was with the outfit, but he was smart. Because either the first or the second platoons would be the point. The fourth platoon, was they had weapons, and we got out of the Hurtgen Forest. We were close to Hawken (ph), which was a city a little bigger than McClain, used to see the most fabulous night displays from the -- the British would only bomb at night. The Americans would bomb during the day and they had that Nordic bomb site or whatever it was, and the devastation that they could do was fantastic, but they had night fighters, and every gun, even our regular machine guns, you had four regular bullets and then one was a tracer, so that you would know if you're going on your thing and they did that with the 20 mm and that for the fighter planes and so on at night. And it was like a show. But when the Battle of the Bulge started, they moved us from there, down into a place called Monschau, which is the northern tip of the Bulge, and we stayed all winter, because when the Bulge started, the 16th of December, something like that, and the only way they could get to us is if they could shoot a mortar, come straight down, and we had troops all around. In fact, Winston Churchill's daughter was a reporter, and she came to, down to our battalion company headquarters was down in Monschau, and she said, "I would like to see how they take a pill box," so they did, and they called this one kid from the mortar platoon, he said, "Is there any pill boxes up there that we haven't taken yet?" He said, "There's a couple." So they got the division artillery, and everything, and they ended up, and they figured they had over 800 pieces of artillery, mortars and everything else that would make sure that they'd give up, and then we still could take your 155 howitzers as a last resort, because you destroy their hearing and everything else with the noise that they would make, but anyway, they did and they took her within seeing, and so on. "Thank you very much, fellas." [ LAUGHTER ] Because today, man it would have been something if, you know, the way they allow the news and all, you didn't see any of them. The guy that's on "60 Minutes," he used to write for the Stars and Stripes, the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Andy Rooney, I believe?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, that's right. He said we weren't allowed to do anything like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you weren't directly involved in the Battle of the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Oh yeah. We captured a hell of a lot of Germans that had American uniforms, and the 106th, it was one of the high ranking numbered divisions, that were decimated, and this colonel became a general, later on. Schmitt was our regimental commander. He ended up with about six regiments all told. Any of these guy that were without commanders and so on, he took them over. And it was fascinating, and you couldn't get air support for about the first six days, and when I first got taken up there to go down to Monschau, there was the roads were, in a town in Belgium, called Verviers. Everywhere you looked there were forests and these 90 mm antiaircraft guns were pointed straight down the road, in case the Germans would break through because they wanted to go to Liege in Belgium. That was a big supply city. They stopped them cold. But then when that was over, we were back up near Bonn, the western capitol of Germany, then the Remagen Bridge come along, and that's where we got, that's, that was really something to run across that bridge and don't know if it's going to be shelled or dropped into the river, which it did eventually, and this Sergeant Epstein called me about the third day into that, and we had troops all up on top. There was a tunnel on the east side that went through a mountain that was maybe five, six hundred foot high and that went through that, the tunnel, and that's, that was a railroad bridge, actually, but you could walk it. They had walks and so on, and then once we took it, we had the MP's were stationed there, and the only way you come back is if you were severely wounded or something like that. Then they built the pontoon bridges, run right at the bridge, and then one by about 3/4 of a mile down the Rhine, in case this one blew up or it became useless when the bridge finally collapsed, as they had on both sides of the river, north and south, on both sides, they had antiaircraft 50 mm quadruples on the 6 by 6 trucks and then they had tanks with 37 mm guns and so on, and the concussion is what really knocked the bridge down. And the first airplanes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Jets?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Jets is where we saw them there, and we had cover with the P39's, the gold fuselage, and they would try to chase these jets. They're standing still. Shhhhhh (indicating noise) and they got some jets later on, but the one thing about it, they had to go up the river, or down the river to bomb. Because of the mountain where the tunnel was, they couldn't go straight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because they couldn't pull up fast enough?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No. And the antiaircraft, see you, with the antiaircraft, you could shoot it in grids. They had to get through it. You know, like when they teach you on shooting for antiaircraft and so on, the fall, what they would do is they had so many guns and they were a mile in each direction, north, south, and then both sides of the river. They'd just grid everything, and you couldn't miss them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fly into it?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Fly, they knocked them out of the air all the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many jets could you see? Were there just a couple or?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Four or five, I would say. They were just starting on them, and I understand that they had them in other parts of Europe, but that's the first time we ever saw them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you when the war ended?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Me, I was in Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That is right. Where was your unit?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Dessau. Peace and occupation.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were on leave in Paris, right?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: 72 hour. It's not counted as leave. 72 hour pass.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A pass to Paris?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: It took about three, six weeks to get to Frankfurt, we went down, they moved, this castle was close to Nordhausen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Nordhausen?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Then here, Dessau.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They were at Dessau?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: That is where we were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did it take to you get to Paris from there?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: They took us by truck to Belgium, then we got on old wooden cars and just sit upright and sleep while you're sitting upright, and took about 10 hours to get down into Paris. Then they delouse you, and I told you about seeing those soldiers that were prisoners in the salt mines.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, tell that again. I don't know if we recorded that.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: That was in Paris at the N'dgare (sp), and they were unloading these guys. They were like these dead guys, just as skinny as them, and then there was a movie star, trying to think of his name, he was in full uniform, and I'm looking at him, he says, "Yeah, I'm he." [ LAUGHTER ] Then they took us, deloused us, gave us new uniforms, and everything else. Everything closed up except the beer joints and the whore houses. Those people were great for taking siestas in the afternoon for two hours, something like that, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All these places closed when the war actually came to an end? Is that what you were saying? So were you there at VE day?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, we got in there at VE day. As we were sitting in this Dessau for two weeks, and I, myself and a few friends, went to Paris and then the whole outfit moved down to southern, not too far from Munich and beautiful country and I think I'm probably the only person that did that, formed my own company. I called it J company. You know there's no J company in the service?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why is that?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Too easy to get mixed up with I or L, I guess. I guess they had a lot of mistakes with that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what did you actually do when you got the official word in Paris? What did you do to celebrate?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Got drunk. [ LAUGHTER ] The hotels, nothing cost you. They had the finest subway system in the world. You could ride their subways. You could do the same thing in England. You didn't pay for any of your public transportation. The government picked it up. But then when we went to go home, I had the opportunity to go down to the Riviera for a week, and I thought, "What the hell do I want to go down there for?" I haven't been home for over three years -- 37 months, something like that. And there was rumors that we were going to be flown home, but the weather got bad, they said, so they took us to what they used to call replacement camps, and they changed the name, and debarkation camps to come back to the states, and we stayed there for two weeks, and then finally, they put us on a liberty ship, and that thing, I think, could go maybe 7 or 8 knots probably is all. It took forever and they landed us up in Boston, and you will get a kick out of this. We captured about 2,000 or 200,000 German soldiers. The elite, the guys were all 6'2", so on, built, 200 pounds and so on, and they said, "Before you do anything, go to the mess hall and you will get a nice big steak dinner." So I go in there and I put my mess kit out and there's this guy about 6'2", and he's overweight now, but when they were in the German Army, they were the prime and he throws this T-bone steak on my mess kit, and he says, "Welcome back, sucker!" [ LAUGHTER ] Because he knew that we were from the division that captured them, and they, the ones that they moved to the United States, or to England, these guys had it great. We used to use English, in England, the Italian or German soldiers, in real dark heavy roll, but there was a big PW mark on the back, but they had free reign in England, especially. They had worked them in the factories and different things like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: One of them was waiting on you back then?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, "Welcome back, sucker!"

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting when you got back?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No. No. Our family was very -- I have a bundle of letters that I wrote home. My mother and my dad wrote me every other day, and my mother always would put a little PS on the bottom, and then she quit. And I kept asking my dad, "What's wrong with mom?" And he said, "She's fine." I said, "No, she isn't. She always put a paragraph at the bottom of the letters." So I wrote a letter to my sister, she wrote at least once a week, and I said, "Now don't bullshit me. What's wrong with mom?" I told her why, and she said, "She's got cancer." That was the biggest blow that I had. When I come home, they were down at the church, something like the thing that the Immaculate Conception puts on, they had a fund raiser, and she was there, and when she walked in, it was like somebody hit me in the chest. I expected it, but when you see it, you just don't know. Oh yeah, there was one I didn't tell you about, used to be my, he was a machine gunner when I first joined the 9th Division, kid by the name of Jake Goss, helluva nice boy, and we were all in a circle, in an opening deciding where we're going to put the perimeter for the night, and he is standing right next to me and all of a sudden, he drops. And we look at him, and here, a sniper put a bullet right through his eye, and at that time, you weren't allowed to declare them dead or anything until the officer that picked up the dead. All you had to do or were allowed to do was send in an overlay on the map where that body was and how he got killed or something like that, but anyway, about three days later, I get a call from somebody. "How come Sergeant Goss has a black and blue mark across his forehead?" I said, "Did you look at his right eye?" He said, "No." I said, "He got shot through the eye." A bunch of us were in a circle, and whoever was the guy that was the sniper, picked on him. Why they picked on him? Why didn't they pick on me or somebody else? But that always, I always had a bad memory about that one. But if you took every one to heart, you had to have a tough skin, or it would bother you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see, one of them was going to be, we talked about Patton.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, El Guettar, I had a machine gun, and I was in the machine gun squad that was sent to -- an idea of El Guettar, was where the Atlas Mountains were right there. We were right at the foot hole -- foothills. The Germans were up there and they had guns and everything else in the caves up at the top of the mountain, and if you moved in the daylight, they'd bring something out and shoot at you, let you know that they were watching you, and Patton come in this day, maybe we were, we had about 26 days in El Guettar, doing nothing but making sure that they didn't shoot you, but they killed quite a few people every day, two or three people that were dug in to slit trenches. There was no such thing as a fox hole. It was all slit trenches. You slept in it and everything else.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You couldn't dig into the ground for a fox hole?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: It was almost like granite. Somewhere, similar to the ground that you see in Afghanistan and so on. Just desolate country. The only thing that grew was in the flat parts, like, I don't know if anybody mentioned the wadis, dry wadis. They were dry rivers, nine months of the year. Two months of the year there was rain, that was their wintertime, in December, January, February, and this is where they hid all these tanks they was talking about, and all of a sudden, they come up out of nowhere, looked like a perfectly straight, level piece of ground, five, six miles wide, and they come out, about 500 tanks, and our 3rd Battalion troops were following behind with them, and we were just like we were in a football stadium watching what was going on down there, and then all of a sudden, boom, boom, knocked out about five tanks, in a couple minutes. Then all of a sudden, somebody gave a whistle or whatever, and they all disappeared. Where in the hell did they go? It looked like from where we were that it was perfectly level and so when the Germans did retreat, we went over that area, and then used the force march and start moving them up towards Tunisia, but these dry wadis, you could hide. Some of the things were sandy soil, and the heavy torrential rains, whatever way they would curve, you had some walls in the wadi that were 20, 30 foot high. You could hide probably couple thousand tanks in that, just the area that we could see. We had young fellas that were laying in these slit trenches, as we called them, and if the shell hit right, they were dead. We had a lot of casualties in there, and we tried one attack. This was right before General Patton came to our battalion headquarters and they were going to attack during the daylight, and the first sergeant was an ex-2nd Division soldier that took over when they reactivated the 9th Division, and he said, "When I blow the whistle, you go over this hill," and you don't know what the hell was there, and I'm all gung ho, and he blows the whistle, and our squad sergeant said, "Come on, go," and he's just laying there and a young kid by the name of Jake Daws from Virginia somewhere, he said, "When that big hunky son-of-a-bitch goes over there, we go over," and he grabbed me back by the seat of the pants. But we never went over, as we lost a couple kids on a previous attack, and just impossible to run in and run through the fire. They had everything zeroed in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let me make sure I have this clear. Were there enemy tanks in the dry wadis? Those were your tanks?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No, they were General Patton's tanks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Patton's tanks?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: He says you wait until you see that show and my boys will show you what's going to do. I think somewhere I got it, where the German will be kaput. Well, they weren't kaput, but the British are coming from the east, and pushing on, and the 1st and 9th division, and I don't know, maybe the 3rd and 45th, there were about four American divisions there, and they eventually squeezed them up into Al Guettar was here. Kasserine was here. Tunisia was here. And you had the Mediterranean Sea and I got wounded five days before the war ended. That's the only thing, time I missed. I got a piece of mortar fragment in this left arm, and I had to walk about four or five miles out of the mountains. Everything was mountains there. Mountains or the red grapes they grow. I think they lived on wine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So where did that happen? Where did you get wounded?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: In Kasserine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Kasserine Pass?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was pretty brutal, Kasserine Pass?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: We just come in their fire once and that is where we got hit with mortars, and my best buddy -- but he jumped, and I was in my slit trench, and he jumped in, and I was laying like this. His head landed here. I got hit here. He's lucky, but it could have knocked a couple eyes out or something like that. But it was a numbing effect. I didn't feel anything, and he said, "I heard something" and he said, "Are you hit?" to me. "I don't think so." Then we look and he could see a little hole in my field jacket. And I didn't hurt, and after the shelling stopped, the other guy, a couple others that were wounded a bit, so the five -- four or five of us that were wounded walked out, out of the mountains down to the first aid station. And then we got, were put on trucks, or ambulances, and taken up to ORAN in the hospital, and then, it started to hurt, and they give you what we used to call blue heaven. Take you about this high off the ground. [ LAUGHTER ]

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was in blue heaven?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: I have no idea, but it did the trick. And it took about two weeks before I got full use of the arm. We had seven months in England before the invasion, and we only had one week of maneuvers, because we had 19 months overseas, and the only thing is your money, because they had lots of beer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah!

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: And the people were friendly. They were very nice. That was a good tour. And then we were on the liberty ships that would take us close enough to get on the little invasion things, on D-day, and we went in about D plus 4 or 5, I'm not sure, I would have to look it up, and when we went, unloaded, we went on the Utah Beach and went straight into combat because we came prepared for combat, and went down near Saint Mere and Galice where the 82nd paratroopers got the hell chewed out of them and I remember distinctly they said, "Don't shoot at anything that is on your left. That is the paratroopers," and that happened for maybe a full day and a half, and then all of a sudden, "Shoot at anything."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: But we got strafed by our own Air Force, and our first five casualties were by our Air Force and that is the most awesome thing is to listen to those 50 caliber, you know they had eight; four on each side, and hedgerows would be a protection, would depend upon which hedgerow, what side you were on, whether you were exposed to it or not, but we had five people that were wounded, but not killed. And then they, that was a trial and error, then after that happened, they assigned an Air Force liaison officer that had direct radio contact and we had no problem at all until the St. Lo bombing which we covered pretty well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: But after we cut the peninsula, then we went up, headed toward Cherbourg and there was some mean fighting there, and a lot of casualties, but we took a lot of prisoners. Then after Cherbourg, we were given two weeks of rest and recuperation, somewhere between there and we were told that every six weeks, we'd get two weeks off. We never did. [ LAUGHTER ] But that's basically what that was the El Guettar. Something else I don't know if I told you, we were the first troops to travel by the 40 and 8's.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I think we talked about that. You were the first troops to do that?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was in North Africa?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Right. We traveled from Port Lyautey, to Oran in 482 miles, according to that book.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now Morocco, were you fighting the Vishy French for a while?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: Two three days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not much?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: No, there was a General Clark that, General Mark Clark, I understand he had a bunch of CB's went in and talked with the French and it was pretty well concluded that they would not give us much opposition. After we had gone ashore and halfway up the hillside, we had no resistance from the French, and because we used to build campfires in Port Lyautey and stuff like that because the Germans weren't interested in anything that were there. We were bivouacked in a cork forest which was actually oak trees that were trimmed, and the bark was that thick, and just skin them off and bottle of their wine would make the cork.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You drink a lot of wine there?

sp.speaker: John T. O'Donnell, Jr.
sp.p: I did, and then I quit, because we could take, we could send somebody from our camp to the winery. They were all over the place. And for $1, you would get a 5 gallon GI gas or water can filled up with wine, and when they start running out of it, they were selling you what they called wild wine. It was not aged. It was like drinking wood alcohol, and we had a couple boys that got affected by it pretty badly, and so that, you quit drinking the wine, so you wouldn't survive, so we just quit it. And then Sicily had good wine, and champagne, $10 a gallon, but like I say, if you survived it, it was a good experience. That's why I'm not afraid to talk about it.
